speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to my office. I understand you have a low-grade fever, an itchy rash, and joint pain that started after some antibiotic treatment. Can you tell me specifically which antibiotic you were taking and how long ago you finished the course?

speaker: Patient
text: 8-year-old girl. The patient was brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of low-grade fever, itchy rash, and generalized joint pain. The rash initially started in the antecubital and popliteal fossae before spreading to the trunk and distal extremities. One week ago, she was diagnosed with acute sinusitis and started on amoxicillin. She has no history of adverse drug reactions, and her immunizations are up to date.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for that information. Given the timing after amoxicillin and the specific distribution of the rash, did you notice any swelling of your tongue, lips, or face, or any difficulty breathing? Also, have you experienced any abdominal pain or diarrhea recently?

REQUEST TEST: Complete Blood Count (CBC), Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR), Liver Function Tests.
REQUEST IMAGES: Photos of the rash distribution.

speaker: Patient
text: izations are up to date. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Acute appendicitis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
It sounds like you were told it might be appendicitis, but your symptoms of an itchy rash starting in the elbow and knee folds (antecubital and popliteal fossae) are very characteristic of a different condition. Could you describe the appearance of the rash more closely, and do you have any history of eczema or allergies?

REQUEST TEST: Serum IgE levels, C-reactive protein (CRP).
REQUEST IMAGES: Close-up photos of the rash in the flexural areas.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Amoxicillin-induced Acute Generalized Exanthematous Pustulosis (AGEP). The clinical presentation of a diffuse, itchy rash appearing shortly after antibiotic initiation, combined with normal inflammatory markers on your blood work, strongly suggests this reaction rather than an infection or autoimmune flare. We should stop the antibiotic immediately and switch to an alternative treatment.
